extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of American government; political scientists and legal scholars
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length exposition of the organizational practices, powers, and limitations of the U.S. Congress (House and Senate) and its working relationship with the President and the executive branch, comparing U.S. practice with parliamentary systems. Covers party organisation (whips, caucuses), legislative procedures (divisions, riders), executive exclusion from debate, patronage, impeachment, and the power of the purse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whip's duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The whip's duties are (1) to inform every member belonging to the party when an important division may be expected, and if he sees the member in or about the House, to keep him there until the division is called; (2) to direct the members of his own party how to vote; (3) to obtain pairs for them if they cannot be present to vote; (4) to 'tell,' i.e. count the members in every party division; (5) to 'keep touch' of opinion within the party, and convey to the leader a faithful impression of that opinion; a member in doubt goes to the whip for counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains each concrete function (notice, attendance, vote direction, pairing, counting, opinion-gathering, counsel). Emphasises practical importance: without the constant presence/activity of the ministerial whip government business would be exposed to casual defeats. Also notes ministerial whip handles patronage-related matters (Patronage Secretary to the Treasury).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of whips for effective party action
rubrics_metrics.description: Whips (and their substitutes) are essential to the discipline of parliamentary parties; without them parties cannot act with habitual concert and bring their full strength to bear on divisions. When a new party is formed its first act is to name whips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: whips enable parties—government, opposition, or third parties—to act as coherent blocs on important votes. Historical/organizational note: in England whips are central; their absence in Congress has consequences for party consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional substitute for whips: caucus committee and 'calls'
rubrics_metrics.description: In the U.S. Congress a caucus committee (elected by the majority at the beginning of each Congress) acts as a substitute for whips: its chairman and secretary give notice of important divisions by sending out a 'call' to party members, take steps to have a quorum and a majority present, and may convoke caucuses when prudent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes how caucus committees perform notice, quorum and majority-gathering duties, and convoke closed-door party meetings to decide attitude on grave or doubtful issues. Limits: caucus cannot be used every day; it is a replacement but imperfect substitute for continuous whip organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions for disobedience are extra-parliamentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Disobedience to party requests in Congress cannot be punished within Congress itself except by social penalties; instead it endangers a member's renomination as party managers communicate with local party managers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains enforcement mechanism: social penalties and electoral/nomination consequences rather than formal parliamentary sanctions. Practical implication: party managers use district-level re-nomination pressure to enforce cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative importance of divisions in Congress vs House of Commons
rubrics_metrics.description: A division in Congress affirms or negatives a particular bill or resolution but cannot throw out the executive; thus divisions in Congress lack the sweeping consequence they have in the House of Commons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: majority need not have full strength always at hand; minority has less to gain from mustering every vote; therefore party discipline on ordinary divisions is weaker and caucuses/calls are used selectively for major issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom on minor questions preserves party unity but weakens consistent policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Members are comparatively free to vote as they please on minor questions (or follow a friend's advice), which prevents dissensions and splits in parties but results in a want of consistent policy and causes the legislature to 'move in zig-zags.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade-off identified: loose cohesion reduces factional splits but produces legislative inconsistency because leaders lack authority to bind members on ordinary matters; few opportunities to define/defend divergent positions owing to little serious debating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caucus as democratic substitute for recognized leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of 'going into caucus' is the American substitute for recognized leadership; it has the advantage of seeming more consistent with democratic equality because every member has in theory equal weight, but cannot be used daily and so leaves members free on many questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why caucus is chosen (democratic appearance) and its practical limits (not daily usable), producing unpredictability on ordinary business when caucus has not issued orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate equality and limited centralized leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate jealously guards the equality of its members; no senator has authority beyond exceptional talent and experience; a senatorial caucus (rarely more than fifty persons) is a better working body than a large House caucus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: leadership in the Senate is weaker/formalised than in parliamentary leaderships; caucus size affects efficacy—smaller body better for coordination; exceptional leaders may emerge in crises (example: Thaddeus Stevens in the House during struggle with Andrew Johnson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of executive from debate reduces direct intercourse and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither House now hears members of the executive; when a minister appears before a committee he appears primarily as a witness to answer questions rather than to state and argue his own case; the President and cabinet have no recognized spokesman in either House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects: less interdependence and community of action between executive and legislature than in parliamentary systems; executive is deprived of power to lead and justify administrative acts in debate. Historical exceptions noted (Washington, early ministers, Wilson 1913).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential influence by patronage is covert and suspicious
rubrics_metrics.description: The President can influence members through patronage (giving places, titles, approving or vetoing bills, ministers allotting contracts); this power is considerable but covert, and knowledge of its use might damage members and expose the executive to imputations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: cut-off of open relations fosters secret influence; secret exertion of influence may be legitimate but is seldom above suspicion. Practical warning about opacity of executive influence mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-binding nature of congressional resolutions and limits of congressional compulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: Either House can pass resolutions calling on the President or ministers to take or refrain from steps, but the President need not obey or even notice them; such resolutions do not shorten his term or limit his discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with parliamentary systems where Commons' resolutions are often treated as imperative because of ability to dismiss the government. Thus Congress's moral or political admonitions lack enforceability absent other mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and practical use of impeachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Impeachment is the heaviest piece of artillery in the congressional arsenal but, being so heavy, is unfit for ordinary use — an extreme remedy designed for political crimes rather than small transgressions; conviction is difficult (Andrew Johnson example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy (hundred-ton gun/heroic medicine) emphasises impracticality for routine control. Practical implication: impeachment is a last resort and does not secure routine cooperation of executive with Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congress cannot compel dismissal of executive officials except by impeachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may investigate, censure, lay down rules for officials and request their dismissal, but if the President stands by his official nothing more can be done; the only formal compulsion is impeachment and conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the limited reach of congressional oversight: political pressure and publicity may force resignations but formal removal requires executive action or impeachment. Analogy to directors forced to keep a manager they distrust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congress's power of the purse constrained by separation and organisation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution grants Congress sole right to raise and appropriate money, but exclusion of the executive from Congress divides the office of Finance Minister among committee chairmen and unconnected committees, leaving important financial business to powerful but not responsible actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: administrative expertise and responsibility are weakened; the administration cannot supervise or ensure consistent, economical financing; fragmentation undermines long-term, coherent fiscal policy. Also notes practical limits of withholding supplies (would injure country) and guaranteed presidential salary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of riders to coerce or constrain the President
rubrics_metrics.description: When Congress cannot lawfully refuse appropriations or lacks the two-thirds to override a veto, it has resorted to attaching 'riders'—provisions unrelated to the appropriation—to money bills in order to force measures upon the President (historical examples: 1867 against Johnson; 1879 against Hayes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the tactic's history and risks: Presidents may veto, and successful coercion depends on margins for veto-override. Notes the practice's development and instances where a President rejected money bills to compel Congress to drop riders.
